description: we are AIDAMS student (CentraleSupélec × ESSEC) with a background in data science and Python. Our team is building ROVER for the terrestrial analogs challenge: click a spot on the Moon, see the best landing points, then fly to the most similar place on Earth to train there.
summary:
ROVER is designed to help researchers navigate beyond our blue planet and venture into the unknown. By giving everyone a personalized way to explore the Moon and Mars, it brings the thrill of space discovery to life without the environmental footprint of physical space tourism. We built ROVER for space enthusiasts who share a deep respect for Planet Earth. 
We built a one-page, interactive 3D mission workspace connecting a mission launcher, an earth site similitudes seeker and an immersive experiment allowing the user to live a mission from the beginning to the end. 
Choose to explore by following a rover, landing where you want or establishing a lunar / martian base. Select an area, inspect measured terrain, find your own path using checkpoints or understand why the mission cannot take place. Compare Earth analog candidates, and prepare a journey using NASA testing sites. 
We used NASA and partner datasets, published research and transparent calculations to create the scientific atmosphere. Our prototype goes through a finite set of Earth sites and separates simulation from field results. The aim is to help teams turn curiosity and ideas into a testable research plan more accessible and easier to discuss.
details:
ROVER: explore there, prepare here

A researcher planning a lunar rover or a future Mars base faces a connected set of decisions: where to land, what to investigate, how to move or deploy equipment, and which uncertainties can be tested on Earth. ROVER brings those decisions into one interactive map. Our vision works in both directions: explore Earth to prepare for the Moon and Mars, and explore the Moon and Mars from Earth through accessible 3D rehearsal.

This addresses “Permanent Moon Base: Locations and Mars” by connecting open planetary and Earth observations to the characterization of terrestrial analogs. Similarity depends on the experiment. A volcanic landscape can help rehearse navigation while failing to reproduce lunar vacuum; a laboratory can test a particular camera or mobility problem under controlled conditions. ROVER makes these differences part of the decision.

One mission, two outcomes

The researcher starts with “Explore with a rover” or “Establish a base”, with human and robotic base options. Both use five consistent stages: Site → Surface plan → Earth test → Journey → Rehearsal & review. Everything remains within the same page, so changing a destination or inspecting a source does not require learning another application.

In Site, researchers choose an area of interest and inspect available terrain. The scientific target and landing point remain separate: an interesting outcrop is not automatically a suitable touchdown location. Elevation, slope and source coverage help identify questions requiring closer investigation.

For a rover, Surface plan connects science stops and a requested return using measured elevation grids and editable scenario constraints. Stops can represent inspection, panoramas or simulated sampling. Terrain-aware routes provide distance and duration estimates, while a separate solar-rover experiment examines how sunlight, battery assumptions and delays can affect a single-stop mission. That experiment does not certify a multi-stop itinerary. For a base, users place landing, base and power areas and compare their geometry. These are conceptual layouts; drawing a power area does not demonstrate enough electricity or safe habitation.

Finding an Earth test

Earth test asks what the team needs to demonstrate. The prototype compares a finite collection of candidate locations using terrain characteristics measured at a shared scale: slope, relief, detrended roughness and local horizon. Purpose-specific priorities make the comparison relevant to a proposed test. A side-by-side view places the planetary target beside an Earth candidate, with a simple dimension chart and a reason to investigate that match.

Temperature, mineralogy and ice evidence appear where available, with their source and spatial context. They influence numerical comparison only when the observations are compatible. Regional geology, a hydrogen signal or a historical temperature range cannot stand in for a local assay or a validated resource supply. Missing evidence remains visible. Researchers can also inspect facilities and analog stations, including relevant capabilities, images, access information and official contact links. Choosing a place creates a test plan; team-reported field observations remain separate from simulated results.

Time connects the journey and the surface plan

Journey combines departure and arrival dates, dated Earth–Moon–Mars positions, transfer calculations and Kennedy-area weather information. The cruise calculation targets the destination’s future position. Recommendations compare sampled date options under disclosed preferences, while forecasts remain unavailable beyond their actual coverage. Watching the journey is optional. The animation supports understanding: cruise is calculated, while launch, atmospheric entry and landing are illustrative stages rather than a flight-ready guidance solution.

Rehearsal lets the team inspect the selected terrain and surface plan in 3D, explore a rover route and review what remains unresolved. The intended output is a clearer shared understanding of the mission and the next Earth experiment to perform.

Science that users can inspect

NASA LOLA/LROC and MOLA/HiRISE products support lunar and Martian terrain. Earth elevation, archival imagery, MODIS surface-temperature observations, planetary environmental products and JPL ephemerides provide complementary evidence. Each answers a particular question at a particular scale.

Our terrain comparison adapts Gower’s numerical similarity and Shepard and colleagues’ scale-aware roughness concepts. Foucher and colleagues’ functional-analog framework informs the focus on the properties needed for each test. Lamarre, Malhotra and Kelly’s lunar rover research informs the separate time-and-energy experiment. These are attributed adaptations; citing a paper does not establish that our rankings reproduce its results. Small information icons show the relevant source, calculation and limitation without overwhelming the main view.

Built for researchers and space lovers

ROVER uses TypeScript, React and Three.js for the browser experience, with Firebase hosting. Python preparation tools process selected scientific datasets; astronomy calculations and background workers support responsive exploration. OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT assisted with research, coding, documentation and checks. Scientific inputs retain their external provenance.

Our creative contribution is the connection between a place, a scientific objective, a surface rehearsal and an appropriate Earth test. The next steps are broader candidate coverage, compatible local environmental observations and independent field validation. ROVER already makes the preparation process visible and approachable, while keeping the evidence needed for stronger conclusions explicit.
